sections.title: 13. Interview Questions
sections.body:
### A. Conceptual Q&A

**Q1. What's the difference between a golden dataset and a benchmark?**
A benchmark (MMLU, HumanEval) is public and general-purpose — it measures how a model compares to the field. A golden dataset is private and domain-specific — it measures whether your system handles *your* users' queries correctly. Benchmarks have wide comparability but low relevance; golden sets have high relevance but no external comparability. You need both, but the golden set is what gates your deploys.

**Q2. What is inter-annotator agreement (IAA), and what's a reasonable target?**
IAA measures how often independent annotators agree on labels, corrected for chance agreement. Cohen's kappa for two annotators, Krippendorff's alpha for many. Target kappa > 0.7; below 0.4 means labels are barely better than chance. Low IAA usually points to ambiguous annotator guidelines, not bad annotators — fix the guidelines first.

**Q3. How many golden examples do you need to detect a 5% regression?**
For a binomial pass rate at alpha=0.05, power=0.8, you need roughly 300 examples per stratum to reliably detect a 5% absolute change. With 50 examples, the noise floor is ~14% — a 5% regression is invisible. The right answer also depends on stratification: 300 total isn't 300 per category.

**Q4. How often should a golden dataset be refreshed?**
Monthly for fast-moving products, quarterly for stable ones — but also event-driven: ship a new feature, detect production distribution shift, discover a new failure mode, or upgrade the model significantly. A stale golden set measures performance against last year's users, which is worse than no eval because it gives false confidence.

**Q5. What is dataset leakage, and why is it fatal?**
Leakage is when golden examples appear (verbatim or near-match) in the training or fine-tuning corpus. The model memorizes them, scores perfectly on eval, and fails on everything else. Always grep the training data for golden inputs before each eval run; use near-duplicate detection, not just exact match, because paraphrased leaks are just as damaging.

**Q6. Why use stratified sampling when building a golden set?**
Random sampling over-represents common categories (password reset) and under-represents rare but important ones (refund disputes, regulated industries). Stratified sampling fixes per-category quotas so every category has enough examples (~30+) to detect its own regressions. Without stratification, your eval silently measures only the dominant category's experience.

**Q7. What's the risk of building your entire golden set synthetically with an LLM?**
Two risks: distribution mismatch (the LLM generates queries that read like LLM outputs, not like real users — your eval measures performance on LLM-flavored queries, not real ones) and label bias (the LLM's expected answers carry its own errors, which your model then gets graded against). Use synthetic data to bootstrap or fill gaps, but anchor the set in production traffic.

**Q8. How would you version a golden dataset?**
Semver-like: MAJOR for schema changes or large rewrites (scores not comparable across), MINOR for added/removed examples (per-stratum counts shift), PATCH for rubric clarifications and metadata fixes (scores comparable). Keep old versions archived so historical eval results stay reproducible. Log every change: which examples, by whom, why.

**Q9. What's the purpose of an adversarial subset inside a golden set?**
Adversarial examples — ambiguous queries, prompt injections, multi-step reasoning, rare languages — are where models actually fail. Tracking them separately prevents a model from quietly regressing on hard cases while preserving the easy-case average. A model that improves on the easy 80% but regresses 20% on adversarial cases will look fine on aggregate and break in production.

**Q10. Why is a 100% pass rate on a golden set a red flag rather than a green light?**
If your golden set scores 100%, the set is too easy — it can't detect regressions because there's nothing left to detect. A healthy golden set scores 80–95%: hard enough that real improvements show up, easy enough that passing is achievable. A 100% pass rate means you need harder examples, not that you're done.

### B. Scenario-Based Questions

**Scenario 1.** Your boss says "we don't have time to build a golden set, just ship the new prompt — it looks better in my tests." Respond in 5–8 sentences.

**Task**: Push back constructively.

**Sample Answer**: I hear the urgency, but "looks better in my tests" is exactly the risk we're taking — five hand-picked queries don't represent our user distribution, and we have no way to detect a regression before users do. The cost of building a minimal golden set is one to two engineer-days: sample 100 production queries, label them with the LLM-assisted + human-review pattern, and run the new prompt against them before shipping. The cost of *not* doing this is the support-bot regression we shipped last quarter — ticket deflection dropped 11% and it took a QBR to notice. I'd rather spend two days now than three weeks undoing damage later. If we truly can't spare two days, let's at least ship to 5% traffic with monitoring and roll back on the first regression signal — but the golden set is strictly cheaper insurance.

**Scenario 2.** Your golden set scores 100% but users complain the bot is unhelpful. What's wrong, and how do you fix it?

**Task**: Diagnose and propose a fix.

**Sample Answer**: Two likely causes. First, the golden set is too easy or too narrow — it covers the queries the bot already handles, not the ones users actually struggle with. Pull production logs, segment by negative-feedback signals (thumbs-down, escalation, re-asks within 60 seconds), and check whether those failure queries are represented in the golden set. If they're not, the set is measuring the wrong distribution. Second, the rubric may be too lenient — "exact-answer match" on a short factual query passes even if the tone is curt, the formatting is wrong, or the bot missed a step the user needed. Replace or augment the rubric with a faithfulness/completeness judge. The fix in both cases: rebuild the golden set from recent production traffic, weight it toward failure segments, and use a stricter rubric. A golden set that scores 100% is not a finished eval; it's an under-powered one.

**Scenario 3.** Your golden set is 6 months old. Production queries now include a new feature (a billing API) and a new user segment (EU customers with GDPR-specific flows) that the set doesn't cover. What do you do?

**Task**: Describe the refresh plan.

**Sample Answer**: This is exactly the trigger for a MINOR version bump. First, sample 100–200 production queries from the last 30 days, stratified by category, with extra weight on the new billing-API and EU-GDPR segments. Deduplicate against existing golden examples so you're not adding near-duplicates. Have the team annotate the new examples with ground truth and rubric — bring in an SME for the GDPR-specific flows because the policy details matter. Add them to the dataset, bump version 1.4.0 → 1.5.0, and re-run the current model against the expanded set to establish a new baseline. Don't compare the new baseline directly to the old — the strata shifted, so any aggregate delta is confounded. Report old strata on their own and new strata separately for at least one quarter, then merge once the new distribution is the steady state.

**Scenario 4.** IAA on your annotation team just measured at kappa = 0.4. How do you diagnose and fix?

**Task**: Lay out the diagnosis and remediation.

**Sample Answer**: 0.4 is barely better than chance — but the problem is almost always the guidelines, not the annotators. First, pull the disagreement set and categorize it: are annotators disagreeing on specific categories, difficulty levels, or rubric types? Usually you'll find 2–3 specific judgment calls (e.g., "is a partial refund answer correct if it doesn't mention the 30-day window?") that account for most of the disagreement. Second, rewrite the guidelines to address those cases explicitly, with worked examples for each side of the call. Third, run a calibration round: have all annotators label the same 50-example set under the new guidelines, measure IAA again, and adjudicate the remaining disagreements with a senior annotator whose ruling becomes a guideline precedent. Target kappa > 0.7 within two calibration rounds. If a specific category still won't converge, that category may need an SME annotator rather than a generalist — some judgments are inherently domain-specific.

**Scenario 5.** You switch from an open-source model to a vendor API and suspect your golden set has leaked into the vendor's training data — your eval scores jumped 18% overnight with no prompt change. How do you confirm and respond?

**Task**: Describe the investigation.

**Sample Answer**: An overnight 18% jump on identical prompts is a strong leakage signal. Confirm with a held-out probe: generate 50 brand-new queries the vendor cannot have seen (current-event questions, internal-codename queries, novel combinations of constraints) and run them alongside the golden set. If the golden set scores ~18% higher than the held-out probe on the same model, leakage is essentially confirmed. Second response: rotate the golden set. Pull fresh production traffic, label it, and replace the leaked examples. Don't reuse the old set for eval — scores are permanently contaminated. Third: report to the vendor; reputable vendors have dedup pipelines and want to know about leakage. Fourth: going forward, maintain a private held-out subset that's never logged, never sent to the vendor in any form, and use it as the ground-truth gate for vendor comparisons. Eval against a possibly-leaked set is worse than no eval because it produces confident wrong numbers.
